query: Reply in 350 words maximum, finish the answer. What official practices verify a Composer package's populated PostgreSQL upgrade separately from a clean install, and an optional private authorization adapter separately from a public no-credential install? Cover preflight refusal, backup/forward recovery limitations, exact locked refs, default-deny and independent policy ownership. Give 4 primary URLs (Composer, PostgreSQL, Laravel, OWASP). Generic question only.

content.text:
Use two independent acceptance paths, not a single “package installs” test:
- Populated-upgrade path: restore a production-shaped PostgreSQL fixture containing prior package schema/data, then run the package’s published migration/upgrade sequence. Test it against a clean PostgreSQL instance separately from the clean-install path. Before any destructive or irreversible step, run explicit preflight checks: supported DB/server versions, extension availability, migration baseline, disk headroom, privileges, lock contention, and a dry run where applicable. Refuse the upgrade with a clear non-zero failure if any predicate is false; never silently rebaseline, truncate, or skip incompatible migrations.
- Clean-install path: start with an empty database and a fresh Laravel application, install only the public package, run migrations, and verify basic public behavior with no credentials, private repositories, environment secrets, or private service bindings present. This proves the package’s public contract is genuinely self-contained rather than accidentally relying on the adopter’s infrastructure.
For PostgreSQL recovery, take and restore-test a logical backup/snapshot before the upgrade. Document that ordinary migration rollback is not a recovery guarantee: destructive DDL/data transformations may be irreversible, and database forward recovery depends on a valid base backup plus continuous WAL archival and a defined recovery target. PostgreSQL’s upgrade guidance also notes that filesystem-level backups cannot substitute for logical dump/restore when changing major versions. Preserve the old cluster/data directory until post-upgrade verification succeeds.
Pin reproducibility at the application level: commit composer.lock, use composer install in CI and production, and assert expected package name/version/reference from the lock file. Composer documents that the lock file records exact resolved versions; explicit dev #commit references have important solver and distribution limitations, so prefer immutable releases/tags plus the committed lock rather than treating a branch pin as a full integrity boundary. ·
Make the private authorization adapter an optional integration: it should be absent from the public package’s required dependencies and only registered through an explicit application-owned configuration/provider. Its absence must produce a safe, deterministic denial—not a missing-class crash or accidental permit. Authorization policy ownership stays with the consuming Laravel application: package code exposes abilities/contracts; the host maps policies and supplies tenant, role, and business rules. Laravel’s Gate supports a default denial response for gates and policies.
Finally, verify all protected endpoints server-side under both configurations: unauthenticated, unauthorized, authorized, and adapter-missing. Default-deny every unmatched ability/resource/action, and require explicit grants; OWASP specifically recommends explicit deny-by-default configuration rather than relying on framework defaults.

Sources:
1. [PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/upgrading.html)
2. [Composer basic usage](https://getcomposer.org/doc/01-basic-usage.md)
3. [Composer schema](https://getcomposer.org/doc/04-schema.md)
4. [Laravel Gate API](https://api.laravel.com/docs/12.x/Illuminate/Auth/Access/Gate.html)
5. [OWASP Authorization Cheat Sheet](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html)
